Despite substantial advances in MTSAD, two key challenges in representation learning remain underexplored: (C1) how to learn scale-robust temporal representations that capture anomalies across different temporal scales and (C2) how to learn global-aware relational representations that capture inter-series dependencies by incorporating series-level global characteristics beyond local windows. To address these challenges, we propose STAGER, a novel method that jointly learns two complementary representations: scale-robust temporal and global-aware relational representations. Specifically, STAGER employs (1) a scale-robust temporal encoder that constructs a multi-scale temporal directed acyclic graph (DAG) to learn scale-robust temporal representations and (2) a global-aware relational encoder that incorporates learnable series-level global embeddings into the temporal representations and models inter-series relationships through graph neural networks. Two complementary auxiliary objectives further enhance the distinctiveness of the global embeddings. Extensive experiments on three real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that STAGER achieves the best average rank among ten evaluated MTSAD methods across three evaluation metrics. Ablation and sensitivity analyses validate the effectiveness of the proposed components and auxiliary objectives, while efficiency evaluations demonstrate that STAGER achieves a favorable trade-off between detection performance and inference time compared with existing methods.

candidates.title: Unifying Partner and Environment Diversity to Improve Human-AI Coordination
candidates.abstract: Real-world applications of modern AI systems require generalization to both unseen environments and novel human users. The field of zero-shot coordination (ZSC) has focused primarily on deploying AI to cooperate with novel partners in otherwise familiar environments. Popular population-based methods achieve this by partnering the agent with a diversity of simulated human users during training in a fixed environment, but does not consider the more realistic scenario where both the users and the environment are unseen during training. Recently, training across environments has been explored in training a single self-play agent, which shows better generalization on both novel human users and unseen environments. In this work, we ask whether jointly modeling partner diversity and environment diversity yields stronger coordination with novel partners in novel environments. We introduce Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across a distribution of procedurally generated environments, and then trains a cooperator policy against this partner population. To further couple social and environmental reasoning, we add a next-state prediction module that encourages representations to encode both partner behavior and task structure. We evaluate CECP on both a neuroscience-inspired cooperative foraging task, and the popular ZSC benchmark Overcooked, under held-out partner and held-out environment conditions. CECP achieves the strongest performance among the compared baselines and attains state-of-the-art results under our evaluation protocol for human-AI collaboration. We analyze the model's latent representation encoded by the next-state prediction module, showing it can not only improve the performance of the cooperative AI, but also provide more interpretable latents, demonstrated by the inference of partner skill levels.

candidates.title: PFedHASNet: A Personalized Federated Hybrid Analog-Spike Network for Multi-Subject Motor Imagery EEG Decoding
candidates.abstract: Motor imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) data are often collected and stored separately across subjects or institutions, and EEG acquisition and annotation remain costly. Training models solely on individual subject data limits the use of information from other subjects, whereas centralizing raw EEG recordings raises privacy and data governance concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw EEG data, providing a practical approach to leveraging information from multiple subjects. Accordingly, we propose PFedHASNet, a personalized federated hybrid analog-spike network for MI-EEG decoding. The shared encoder integrates continuous-valued temporal features, leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) spike responses, and channel-wise log-variance statistics through learnable fusion weights. Client-private residual adapters and classifiers perform subject-specific feature refinement and personalized prediction, respectively. Experiments on held-out trials from participating subjects across four public MI-EEG datasets show that PFedHASNet achieves the highest mean client macro-F1 among 18 model configurations in cross-model comparisons, while maintaining competitive decoding performance with a compact client-side model in comparisons using the same backbone. Ablation studies further examine the contributions of hybrid representations and personalization components to decoding performance.
candidates.comment: 13 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics

candidates.title: Structure-Aware Transformers for Hierarchical Authorization in Personal AI Agents
candidates.abstract: Personal AI agents can carry out complex, multi-step tasks on users' behalf, but doing so often involves numerous permission requests. Manually reviewing each request is time-consuming, while indiscriminate approval poses privacy and security risks. Predicting users' authorization preferences offers a way to reduce this burden while preserving user control. However, authorization prediction is challenging because permission requests are often hierarchical and observed user decisions are sparse and potentially correlated. To address these challenges, We propose the Parent-gated Authorization Transformer for Hierarchies (PATH) to predict users' authorization preferences for personal AI agents. PATH is a novel neural network architecture that combines hierarchy-aware attention masks with a parent-gated probability formulation to ensure hierarchy-consistent predictions. Hierarchy-level embeddings further support learning from sparse observations and patterns shared within each authorization level. We establish finite-sample risk bounds and provide sufficient conditions for consistent authorization probability estimation and algorithmic convergence. Experiments on simulated data, AI-generated user profiles, and real user authorization data demonstrate strong predictive performance with zero hierarchy violations.

candidates.title: RoboHarness-RL: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for VLM-Based Robot Manipulation
candidates.abstract: Agentic harnesses enable frontier vision-language models (VLMs) to manipulate robots through perception, planning, and control tools, yet achieving comparable performance with compact open-weight VLMs remains challenging. We present RoboHarness-RL, an agentic reinforcement learning framework for improving VLM-based robot manipulation through tool calls. Starting from supervised fine-tuning on successful teacher demonstrations, the VLM further improves through multi-turn reinforcement learning with task-outcome rewards, without relying on vision-language-action models or world action models. To support efficient multi-turn training, we develop LiteHarness, which uses hierarchical memory to keep interaction contexts compact while preserving task performance. With Qwen3.5-9B, RL raises success from 31.2% to 44.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 and from 57.8% to 73.3% on LIBERO-Pro; these gains extend to randomized RoboTwin scenes unseen during training (26.4% to 38.0%). Behavioral analysis further shows that RL reduces repetitive-call rates by up to $4\times$, shortens successful executions, and improves recovery from negative feedback. Project page: https://aim-uofa.github.io/RoboHarness-RL/

candidates.title: To Critic Or Not To Critic
candidates.abstract: As large language models tackle longer and more complex tasks, understanding when a critic improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes increasingly important. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains a critic to reduce variance and provide fine-grained credit assignment, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) drops the critic and avoids the bias of bootstrapping from the critic's value estimates. Although recent critic-based methods have reported strong performance relative to GRPO, it remains unclear when each approach is preferable. We argue that there is no universal answer; instead, the choice depends on several interacting factors, including batch size, critic reliance, and task complexity. We study the bias-variance tradeoff in terms of gradient direction, measuring how closely each method's gradient estimates align with the true policy gradient as batch size grows. Under a shared actor objective, we compare GRPO with PPO in control tasks, short-horizon math, and long-horizon terminal agents. Across more than 1,200 training runs, including 96 with LLMs, we find that PPO generally leads at small batch sizes, while GRPO often overtakes heavily bootstrapped PPO and reaches parity with lightly bootstrapped PPO at larger batches. At longer horizons and in more complex domains, GRPO needs larger batches to catch up to PPO's performance. Accounting for training compute, critics pay off at small budgets, but their returns diminish at larger budgets.

candidates.title: Marketing-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Models and Agents on Real-World Marketing Capabilities
candidates.abstract: As frontier AI models and agents are deployed more broadly in the real world, marketing is emerging as one of their largest applications. Marketing teams use AI models to produce brand assets like website copy and social media posts, while consumers' agents autonomously discover products, research purchases, and navigate websites. However, evaluating marketing capability is difficult because unlike areas like software development, customer support, or legal review where ground truth is more objectively defined, marketing is subjective, and output quality is judged based on taste and brand. We introduce Marketing-Bench, the first open-source marketing benchmark, which pairs discriminative tasks (detecting brand anomalies) with generative tasks (remediation), while keeping answers verifiable. Marketing-Bench tests five key pillars: factuality, consistency, coherence, structure, and brand voice, all crucial elements for good brand content on the web. We find that frontier models are far from solving the benchmark: the average model corrects only about half of the introduced issues (53.1%), whereas a marketing expert corrects nearly all of them. Even the strongest, GPT-6 Astra, reaches only 74.8%, with Claude Opus and Fable, Gemini Argon, and GPT-6 Sol falling well short. These findings suggest that marketing capabilities are less mature than adoption implies, and that principled evaluation should precede further scaling of usage. Marketing-Bench is a first step toward "frontier marketing models" with superhuman marketing performance.

candidates.title: TableRouter: Query-Aware Evidence Construction for Long-Table Question Answering
candidates.abstract: LLMs can reason over tables, but when tables outgrow the context budget, retrieving relevant rows is only part of the solution. A retrieved subset may omit information required for an exact aggregate; even complete evidence may remain difficult for an LLM to use. We introduce TableRouter, a training-free framework that analyzes each query, then chooses between two routes: a computation route, which derives question-conditioned statistics from the full table, and a coverage route, which retrieves relevant rows and column summaries. The chosen context is passed to a frozen LLM in one call. Across three LLMs and three large-table benchmarks, TableRouter outperforms the strongest of six single-call baselines in all nine settings by 1.2-18.3 accuracy points, using 77-95% fewer estimated FLOPs than truncated-table prompting, with indexing amortized across questions. The gains extend to long tables from databases not used in earlier experiments, where TableRouter achieves 35.8% with Qwen2.5-7B, versus 16.4% for the strongest external baseline. A controlled experiment shows that explicitly providing computed statistics improves accuracy by up to 40.0 points, even when all answer-determining rows are available. These results distinguish evidence access from evidence use: long-table reasoning depends on how information is represented, not only on which rows are retrieved.
candidates.comment: Submitted to ACL Rolling Review, October 2026

candidates.title: Grounding Language Models in Revealed Audience Behavior
candidates.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to simulate how an audience will respond to a headline or a post, and such simulators are validated against what people say. We validate them against what people do. We call a model grounded in revealed audience behavior when it is fine-tuned on records of what audiences actually clicked, liked or watched, and we ask not only whether asking a model falls short of grounding it, as prior work found, but why and where. Why: the gap is a property of the training signal, not mainly of model size or prompting. The same 8B model is right about half the time when asked which headline readers will click and 86.5% of the time when grounded in the clicks; the strongest prompting we tried only matches a text classifier; a grounded 0.6B model beats every prompted frontier model in our runs; and whether the clicks are fitted as counts or as shares makes no detectable difference in a pre-registered test. The asked 8B model also reproduces stated-preference cues, favoring question headlines that in fact lower clicks. Where: across four behaviors, grounding wins where the text carries the signal (short-video likes, +20 points on 200 pre-registered videos), only ties an asked model given the reader's history (news clicks), and nothing text-only gets far from chance on watch time. Code, adapters and run outputs will be released.

candidates.title: ADE: A Zero-Training Unlearning Method for Latent World Models
candidates.abstract: Latent world models learn compact recurrent dynamics from offline trajectories, yet deployed simulators can retain backdoor triggers or stale transitions from outdated physical regimes. Existing unlearning methods fail in autoregressive physics: gradient updates distort latent manifolds and compound rollout drift, naive output zeroing suppresses valid control responses on trigger onset, and single-step deletion leaves corruption inside recurrent hidden states. We propose Analytical Dynamics Excision (ADE), a deterministic, zero-training closed-form unlearning algorithm for latent world models. Using only cached pretraining moments, ADE recovers retain covariances via single-pass matrix downdating without raw retain data and cascades closed-form edits across the input bottleneck, hidden states, and downstream heads. Pairing orthogonal excision with whitened recurrent damping and mean-preserving affine calibration neutralizes out-of-manifold backdoors and realigns in-manifold shifts without variance collapse. Across four regimes on three MuJoCo benchmarks, ADE outperforms seven tuned baselines on DreamerV1, eliminating HalfCheetah and Hopper velocity-flip triggers $4.4\times$ faster than fine-tuning, and transfers zero-shot to DreamerV3.

candidates.title: Metric-Dependent Scaling Laws for Sketched Multiclass Softmax Regression
candidates.abstract: We study scaling laws for full-batch gradient descent with general stable deterministic learning rates in sketched multiclass softmax regression. In a Gaussian teacher student model with power law feature and teacher spectra, the student observes a random feature sketch and reuses a finite labeled sample throughout optimization. Sketching generally makes the student misspecified, so the analysis must jointly account for approximation, nonlinear finite time learning, and the fixed empirical perturbation induced by data reuse. On an exponentially likely sketch event, we show that cross entropy excess and excess zero one risk share a common spectral scale, consisting of a resolution term and an effective learned dimension divided by sample size; teacher student decision disagreement follows the square root of that scale. The resulting balance gives rate optimal sketch and cumulative horizon choices, and synthetic experiments support the predicted regimes and metric dependent exponents.

candidates.title: How Much Dependency Can a Marginal Rule See? Total Correlation in Diffusion LM Parallel Decoding
candidates.abstract: A masked diffusion language model is fast because it commits several tokens per step. Each token is sampled from its own marginal, so the dependency between the tokens is lost, and the size of that loss is the conditional total correlation C of the committed set. Most decoders choose the set from per-position marginals, which can bound C but cannot determine it. We ask how well they predict it. We estimate C for fixed candidate sets on four masked diffusion LMs from two families. On three of the four, the best marginal-only predictor is off by about one bit (0.74 to 1.17), 1.8 to 3.7 times less than a baseline that knows only the bound, and most of this accuracy comes from the bound itself. On a subset, our estimate ranks sets like the exact KL cost of a parallel commit, but sits a median 0.4 to 1.1 bits below it on prose and when the rest of the text is still masked. Dream-instruct is the exception, mainly on prose, where its conditionals are least self-consistent. Among six common marginal rules, pooling over the set beats gating on its weakest position in all 24 paired comparisons. The measurement needs a validated readout: Dream and LLaDA place a position's prediction at different logit indices, and the wrong index inflates an inconsistency diagnostic 14 to 41 times. We give three checks that measure the convention. Our results concern predicting C for a fixed set, not what a dependency-aware decoder gains.
candidates.comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Diffusion Language Models: Foundations, Efficiency, and Reasoning (DiffuLM). Code: https://github.com/DovudAsadov/dllm-total-correlation

candidates.title: Discovering Bandwidth-Efficient Prefetchers to Shrink the Cache Hierarchy
candidates.abstract: Shared last-level caches (LLCs) increasingly dominate server processor die area, forcing architects to trade core counts for cache capacity. While intelligent data prefetching offers a pathway to reclaim this silicon, designing coordinated, multi-level prefetching policies for multi-core systems is bottlenecked by day-long, cycle-level simulations. This simulation wall limits even LLM-based microarchitecture discovery; the state-of-the-art ArchAgent system evolves one cache level at a time on single-core benchmarks, adds multi-core configurations only at the end, and trails the human champion under multi-core shared cache contention. We introduce DuoArchitect, an autonomous agentic framework for multi-fidelity, multi-core co-discovery of prefetchers. Agents jointly evolve evaluation proxies and coordinated prefetching policies across the L1D, L2, and LLC hierarchies, constructing simulation proxies 3-26x faster than cluster evaluation and hardware diagnostic oracles to guide the search. To study how much cache silicon a smarter prefetcher can replace, we evaluate and evolve prefetchers under reduced cache budgets, and find that evolving under our tightest cache constraint (with both the L2 and LLC halved) produced our strongest prefetcher overall at every cache size we tested: DuoArch-Nano. On the Fourth Data Prefetching Championship (DPC4) benchmarks with full-size caches, DuoArch-Nano delivers a 9.2% geomean IPC speedup (+10.5% on four-core mixes) while reducing four-core DRAM traffic by 11.4%, more than doubling the gains of the human champion BertiGO and the agentic ArchAgent v2. When the LLC is halved, DuoArch-Nano erases the baseline's 8.6% overall slowdown and edges out the full-LLC baseline overall (+0.88%), showing that agentic frameworks can generate prefetchers that reclaim megabytes of LLC SRAM per core with zero overall IPC penalty.

candidates.title: Reading, Writing and Repairing Game-Theoretic Policies in Weight Space
candidates.abstract: Can a language model work in the weight space of a policy network for a repeated game? We put four questions to a mid-size open model, on recurrent networks of 1{,}218 weights with exactly checkable answers. Given a population of opponents described in English, write a policy that is optimal: its value is a finite computation over the agent's information state, so a submitted network has an exact gap from the optimum. Given a network's weights, report its action after each of fifteen opponent histories; recover the state machine it implements, judged on every opponent sequence to depth ten; or repair a network whose output was altered in one place and say which round first goes wrong. The model recovers the program in 62 of 66 replies, reports all fifteen behavioral entries correctly in 34 of 36, and attains the optimum in 20 of 20 when it states a policy the evaluator compiles. Repair is the exception: 4 of 18 repaired, 5 of 18 diagnosed, with a median patch covering one of the two entries needed.

candidates.title: Localizing Cross-Lingual Generalization in Parameter Space
candidates.abstract: Cross-lingual transfer is uneven across tasks, succeeding for natural language understanding but often failing for mathematical reasoning. We argue that this asymmetry is governed by the geometry of parameter space. Specifically, cross-lingual generalization is determined by whether English and target-language LoRA adapters share a low-error basin. To test this, we use linear mode connectivity (LMC) between English and target-language adapters, evaluating on three tasks. We find that NLI and QA model-language pairs are mostly linearly connected, whereas mathematical reasoning (Math) pairs are not, indicating that basin geometry is task-dependent. Such disconnection in Math is ``local'' rather than global. A small target-language task sample, applied only to the English adapter's language encoding or semantic composition layers, is enough to repair it. Cross-lingual generalization is also factorizable into language-specific encoding and language-agnostic composition, each supplied separately from a cheaper signal. English task data routed to the composition layers and an unlabeled target-language corpus routed to the language encoding layers each alleviate it on their own for nearly every pair. Composition is the more influential of these, and it needs no target-language data. Together, these results suggest that cross-lingual generalization decomposes into language-specific and language-agnostic components in parameter space. This decomposition offers a practical route for low-resource cross-lingual adaptation.

candidates.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?
candidates.abstract: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.

candidates.title: Predict Backbone, Graft Dynamics: A Decoupled Paradigm for Time Series Forecasting
candidates.abstract: Modern long-term forecasters are typically optimized for point-wise accuracy, which rewards dominant low-frequency backbones but often suppresses high-utility local dynamics such as abrupt variations, transient surges, and turning points. We propose Predict Backbone, Graft Dynamics, a decoupled forecasting paradigm that separates stable structural prediction from grounded dynamic restoration. We instantiate it as GRAFT, where a base forecaster predicts the reliable trajectory backbone, and a dedicated grafting path restores historically recurrent dynamics through retrieval-based evidence, phase-aware release, channel-wise control, and restoration-cooperative optimization. Unlike generic post-hoc revision methods that correct residual errors, GRAFT formulates the second stage as grounded dynamic grafting, where historical response evidence is calibrated into transferable dynamics and selectively grafted onto the backbone under phase-, channel-, and confidence-aware constraints. Across the full evaluation grid of seven benchmarks, two metrics, four horizons, and six backbones, GRAFT improves over the corresponding backbone in 87% of all comparisons, with average MSE/MAE reductions of 4.6%/3.9%. Dynamic-window analyses show that GRAFT restores local dynamics while preserving the stable backbone structure. These results suggest a new principle for high-utility forecasting: predict the backbone, then graft the dynamics.

candidates.title: DexOPD: Dual-Extrapolation On-Policy Distillation for Diffusion Models
candidates.abstract: Flow-based diffusion models have become a mainstream paradigm for text-to-image generation, where task-specific post-training produces specialist models with complementary strengths. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (OPD) offers an efficient way to consolidate these specialists into a single unified student. Recent methods strengthen supervision through teacher extrapolation, constructing stronger proxy teachers that allow distilled students to surpass the original specialists. However, their extrapolation directions remain defined solely by frozen teacher and reference models, leaving the student's own training progress unexploited. To address this limitation, we introduce DexOPD, a dual-extrapolation on-policy distillation method for diffusion models. DexOPD retains extrapolated teacher supervision while leveraging a lagging historical student as the reference for student self-extrapolation. Sampling across multiple self-extrapolation gains from shared initial noise broadens exploration along the student's evolving trajectory, and task rewards convert pairwise differences in candidate quality into a normalized auxiliary regression direction. Empirically, we evaluate DexOPD on GenEval, OCR, and DrawBench. The resulting unified SD3.5-Medium student achieves a GenEval reward of 0.9736, an OCR score of 0.9515, and a DrawBench Aesthetic score of 6.4875, surpassing the corresponding specialist teachers as well as all evaluated OPD and multi-task reinforcement learning baselines across these three benchmarks while preserving standard single-model inference.

candidates.title: On the Information Loss of Multi-Token Prediction: Origin and Solution
candidates.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) accelerates autoregressive decoding through block-wise prediction, but remains vulnerable to error accumulation across sequentially generated blocks. To investigate this limitation, we analyze the distinction between block-wise and sequence-level cumulative information loss (CIL). Specifically, when the model generates using its own previous outputs without access to reference answers, the input-conditional gap equals the cross-block dependence of the reference targets. To improve prediction when these generated prefixes are imperfect, we propose Dual-MTP, which supervises shared prediction heads under full and randomly masked contexts. Together, complete-prefix supervision and context perturbations provide complementary training signals while retaining the MTP architecture. To characterize this training objective, we use the normalized dual loss to bound the divergence between the model's predictive distributions under full and masked contexts. Experiments across five backbones and six tasks spanning mathematical reasoning and GLUE understanding show that Dual-MTP achieves the highest average task score on four of five backbones, with gains of up to 2.46 points over MTP. On mathematical reasoning tasks, Dual-MTP also achieves 1.4 to 1.9 times the decoding throughput of the NTP reference. Together, these results show that dual-context supervision can improve prediction accuracy while retaining efficient multi-token decoding.

candidates.title: Sounding the Black Box: Online Training of Embedded Neural Networks in Forward-Only Physical Simulators
candidates.abstract: Hybrid physics-neural simulators embed neural networks in partial differential equation (PDE) solvers to model unresolved subgrid dynamics while preserving resolved physics and conservation laws. Because closure outputs feed back across time steps, single-step offline regression does not directly minimize multi-step rollout error, motivating online trajectory optimization. Solver backpropagation through time (BPTT) is the standard online solution when solver derivatives are available, yet many operational Fortran and C/C++ simulators expose only non-differentiable, forward-only interfaces. We introduce FORGE (Forward-Only Response and Gauss-Newton Estimation), an online framework that trains embedded networks from forward runs alone by decoupling exact network derivatives from black-box simulator dynamics. Stage I warms up the rollout via a low-dimensional Gauss-Newton step along output-orthonormal weight directions, canceling multi-layer feature drift via a final-layer correction. Stage II perturbs spatial output fields to fit a gain-bounded causal linear response operator across rollout steps, solves for regularized target outputs, and updates all weights via network backpropagation. Across five 2D and 3D benchmarks spanning phase separation, reaction-diffusion, fluid and MHD turbulence, and ocean circulation, FORGE outperforms gradient-free, reinforcement-learning, and emulator-based baselines, cutting coarse-solver test mean squared error (MSE) by 50%-96% in 2D and 70% in 3D, outperforming the strongest forward-only baseline by 16%-69%, and recovering 88%-98% of Solver BPTT's gains. Code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/FORGE.

candidates.title: Perception Is Enough, at the Right Scale: Scale-Adaptive Token Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
candidates.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models must process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting computational cost limits real-time robotic control. Token pruning reduces this cost, but a fixed semantic scale of perceptual representation can overlook information needed at different stages of manipulation. We show that perceptual semantics can guide effective token selection without relying on internal attention when the selection scale adapts to the scene's evolving semantic structure. Based on this observation, we introduce TauPrune-VLA, a training-free method that controls the scale of the retained perceptual representation through a single perception temperature $τ$. To adapt this scale as manipulation proceeds, TauPrune-VLA updates $τ$ online using trends in perceptual semantics, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating the adjustment strength. While these semantics evolve over the course of manipulation, they remain relatively stable between consecutive frames. This continuity allows retention indices computed from the current observation to be applied at the next policy invocation, enabling token selection to run asynchronously with inference and reducing pruning overhead. Evaluated across diverse VLA models and simulation benchmarks, TauPrune-VLA achieves up to a $1.86\times$ inference speedup while maintaining near-baseline task success rates. We further validate its effectiveness on two real-world robotic platforms.
candidates.comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Project page: https://lin0e0.github.io/TauPrune-VLA/

candidates.title: MELODI: Similarity-Identity Decoupling for Lightweight Ranking
candidates.abstract: For latency-constrained candidate ranking, we propose a similarity-identity decoupling framework that separates target-history compatibility from target-only information. We study two orders for computing pooled similarity, similarity-then-pool and pool-then-similarity, and identify linearity of the similarity operator in its history argument, for each fixed target, as sufficient for their equivalence, justifying the cheaper pool-then-similarity form. We instantiate the framework as multi-head efficient lightweight operator for decoupling identity and similarity (MELODI), whose similarity branch combines target-conditioned multi-head history pooling with a single residual-free cross layer that is linear in its pooled-history input and whose identity branch is problem-dependent. On public benchmark datasets, MELODI matches or surpasses the evaluated target-aware and target-agnostic baselines. On two large-scale industrial datasets, its area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), normalised discounted cumulative gain (NDCG), and recall values are equal to or higher than those of the evaluated target-aware baselines. Processor measurements show lower latency than the evaluated candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts, further reduced by request-local history reuse.

candidates.title: Beyond the Last Loop: Reinforcement Learning with a Teacher Extrapolated from the Model Itself
candidates.abstract: Looped language models apply one shared transformer stack several times per token, and every loop can be read out through the shared language-model head. Post-training them with verifiable rewards is hard: the outcome reward carries one bit per response, spreading it over loops trains intermediate loops on tokens sampled from the last loop, and distillation needs either a teacher that ignores the reward or an external, larger model. We observe that a looped model already contains a teacher stronger than its last loop: the next-token distribution extrapolated from the first loop through the last. ELGO (Extrapolated-Loop Group-relative Optimization) adds to GRPO a dense per-token distillation term towards this distribution. The teacher is computed from an anchor copy of the model, which stays frozen and is replaced by the current model once the student's KL to the teacher falls below a threshold, so the teacher improves with the student without chasing its own extrapolation. The outcome reward splits probability between correct and incorrect responses, and the teacher decides which tokens are preferred inside a response. Between refreshes the objective is KL-regularised RL anchored at the teacher, whose optimum tilts the teacher by the reward. On Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, ELGO raises the average avg@8 over five math benchmarks from 62.32 with GRPO to 64.20 and is the best compared method on every benchmark, while spreading the reward over loops falls below the base model.

candidates.title: CAPE: Coordinating Calibration and Search for Tool-Use Policies
candidates.abstract: A tool call can fail even when the operation behind it is correct, because the receiving tool parses delimiters, dates or record layouts under a configuration the agent cannot inspect. Compiling a tool-use policy for such a tool requires both calibration, which evaluates candidate calls on candidate configurations, and search over the evaluated calls. The two share one compilation budget: calibrating everything first postpones any improved policy until the end, while re-solving every partially known model delays the next useful query. A call becomes usable as soon as its effects are known on the configurations that reach it. We present CAPE, a training-free compiler built on this observation. It maintains an executable policy at all times, directs calibration to the calls that can improve this policy, and tightens bounds only where doing so ends calibration early. Returned policies preserve every configuration the initial policy completes, and CAPE certifies optimality when its executable and optimistic values meet. On CSV and JSON workflows built from 64 requests, CAPE reaches the independently computed optimum in 502 of 504 compilations while taking 22.0% less compilation time than eager exact search. On larger CSV families it returns policies with higher completion at similar compilation time, and it raises completion by 15.38 to 34.66 percentage points over an LLM that revises its serialization from error feedback.

candidates.title: Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation for LLM Unlearning
candidates.abstract: Large language model unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data while preserving unrelated model capabilities. Existing likelihood-based methods commonly optimize against fixed forget sequences, providing only negative supervision on what the model should not generate and overlooking the states visited by the evolving unlearned policy. We introduce Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation (CPSD), a new unlearning framework that constructs an explicit knowledge-reduced target distribution and distills it along the model's own trajectories. Given a student rollout, a frozen reference model evaluates each token under a plain context and a privileged context containing the forget information. CPSD treats the resulting distributional shift as a knowledge-associated direction and reverses it to obtain a counterfactual unlearning target. The student is then trained to match this target at every rollout position while retaining its utility on unrelated data. We further introduce a privacy-enhanced variant that combines distributional unlearning with lightweight sequence-level suppression. Experiments under OpenUnlearning show that CPSD improves the forgetting-utility trade-off over NPO across TOFU forget-set sizes and Llama models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters. On MUSE-News, the privacy-enhanced variant improves all reported knowledge, memorization, privacy, and utility metrics over NPO.

candidates.title: Scoring What Matters: Exact Feedback Reduction for Language Model Comparison
candidates.abstract: Comparing language-model checkpoints requires estimating performance differences, yet evaluation pipelines can pay to score responses whose contributions cancel from those differences. We introduce Contrast-Aware Feedback Acquisition (CAFA), a sampler-agnostic method that identifies which scores a requested linear report needs before acquiring feedback. CAFA groups identical scoring inputs and aggregates their report coefficients, removing queries beyond ordinary caching while preserving the fully scored result. For a fixed response bank and an otherwise unrestricted scalar scorer, we characterize necessary and sufficient query sets for exact recovery of sample means, either alone or jointly with ordinary sample covariances. On controlled updates, CAFA removes 55.8% and 90.1% of the scoring inputs remaining after caching for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, respectively, averaged over four generation repetitions. Across three online group relative policy optimization (GRPO) trajectories, Independent Star sampling with CAFA achieves 46.1-51.3% lower recorded generation-plus-feedback cost than independent autoregressive sampling with caching at a common empirical precision threshold (RMS MCSE $\leq 0.04$). This is a post hoc comparison of completed runs on a fixed budget grid. All 504 evaluated report cells reproduce the fully scored means and covariances to numerical precision. We provide a modular implementation supporting existing response banks, versioned caches and external scorers.

candidates.title: Learning When a Robot Should Ask For Help: Adaptive Intervention Requests in Human-Robot Teaming
candidates.abstract: Robots operating in complex environments occasionally encounter situations where autonomous navigation fails. Requesting and receiving a timely intervention from their human supervisor can be critical for failure prevention or recovery. However, requesting help too frequently or at inappropriate times can increase operator workload and reduce team efficiency, while delayed requests may lead to prolonged downtime or unrecoverable failures. In addition to alert timing, the human, robot and task context also influences the intervention outcomes. This paper proposes an algorithm for learning to generate adaptive human intervention requests during human-robot teaming. A help-seeking policy is trained via offline reinforcement learning based on past intervention helpfulness and autonomous progress. This learned alert policy enables a robot to selectively request human help when the intervention outcome is likely to be beneficial. We evaluate the proposed policy in different task environments and user expertise levels in simulation, followed by evaluation in a physical user study. Our findings demonstrate that the learned policy improves exploration efficiency, reduces unnecessary alerts, and enhances novice user support without compromising expert performance in real-time human-robot teaming missions.

candidates.title: Rethinking Universal Time Series Foundation Models from Unified Representations to Shared Dynamics (UniTFU)
candidates.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have attracted increasing attention in cross-domain forecasting. Existing works mainly rely on large-scale pre-training and general modeling paradigms. However, the former heavily relies on the diversity and domain coverage of pre-training data. Meanwhile, the latter learns unified representations across heterogeneous domains without explicitly identifying the temporal regularities shared among them, limiting robust cross-domain generalization. This work explores cross-domain generalization by characterizing commonalities in recurring local dynamics across domains, rather than relying solely on implicitly learned temporal representations. To capture such cross-domain commonalities, we propose Time Series Foundation Units (TFUs) as reusable building blocks discovered from multi-scale temporal segments, each characterizing a recurring local dynamic pattern shared across domains. Building on TFUs, we develop a unified time series foundation model (UniTFU) that explicitly reuses and composes shared temporal regularities across domains for forecasting. Experiments on seven public datasets show that UniTFU substantially outperforms existing TSFMs in cross-domain forecasting and can efficiently adapt to target-domain dynamics by updating its reusable components with limited target data. UniTFU also achieves strong forecasting performance compared with state-of-the-art methods.

candidates.title: Meta-Amortized Cognitive Modeling
candidates.abstract: Cognitive modeling is highly iterative. Researchers repeatedly revise model structures, parameterizations, covariates, and experimental designs as theories evolve and data accumulates. Amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks provides rapid estimation for individual models, but every revision requires new simulations and training. Here, we introduce CogFormerV2, a meta-amortized framework that enables researchers to specify, revise, and fit cognitive models with a single network, carrying amortization across an entire space of models all at once. Trained once in about a day on a single GPU, it delivers accurate, well-calibrated posteriors across more than 14.6 billion model configurations spanning binary, multi-alternative, and continuous decisions, with varying parameter sets, covariate structures, trial counts, and contamination levels. It can fit empirical data from distinct behavioral tasks and extends to new models through continual learning and representation transfer. Released as an open-source interactive application, CogFormerV2 provides a reusable infrastructure for meta-amortized inference in cognitive modeling, while carrying the potential to accelerate computational modeling workflows at large.

candidates.title: ReJEPA: Bounded Predictive Regulation for Latent World Models
candidates.abstract: Latent world models learn representations by predicting future states in an abstract embedding space rather than reconstructing raw pixels. When training across multi-frame sequences, however, not all frames and spatial regions are equally informative or predictable. We argue that forcing a world model to minimize every prediction error may be unnecessary and harmful. Under standard $L_2$ loss, unbounded gradients force the encoder and predictor to overfit noisy or transient frames at the expense of core physical structure, while amplifying gradient conflict with representation regularizers. Conversely, $L_1$ loss bounds large gradients, but its constant gradient magnitude near zero disrupts the local smoothness required for planning. We resolve this tension with \textbf{ReJEPA}, a bounded predictive regulation principle that combines bounded gradients for large errors with smooth quadratic behavior near zero, instantiated simply via the element-wise $\log\cosh$ loss. As a drop-in training replacement across Temporal Straightening, LeWorldModel, and V-JEPA~2.1, $\log\cosh$ consistently outperforms $L_2$, a curvature-matched quadratic control, $L_1$, and Smooth-$L_1$ baselines without altering architectures or inference procedures. Notably, the gains grow with environmental complexity, scaling from simple navigation to contact-rich manipulation and real-world autonomous driving on NAVSIM. Probing and geometric analyses confirm that relaxing the penalty on extreme errors yields representations that better capture physical states and align with the true planning cost landscape.

candidates.title: TQ-HQNet: A Trainability-Aware and Qubit-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neural Network for Cross-Domain Learning on Heterogeneous Data
candidates.abstract: Hybrid quantum neural networks are a promising direction for noisy intermediate-scale quantum computing, but their practical effectiveness is often limited by poor trainability, rigid circuit design, and weak robustness across heterogeneous real-world tasks. This paper proposes TQ-HQNet, a Trainability-Aware and Qubit-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neural Network for cross-domain learning on heterogeneous data. The proposed framework combines three mechanisms: 1) adaptive latent compression to map domain-specific features into qubit-compatible representations, 2) trainability-aware search over compact variational circuit candidates, and 3) hybrid fusion of multiple shallow quantum experts to improve robustness without increasing qubit cost excessively. TQ-HQNet is evaluated on four public datasets spanning neurological screening, phishing detection, financial direction prediction, and DNA sequence classification. Across all domains, the proposed model consistently improves over a fixed hybrid quantum baseline, with balanced-accuracy gains of +0.280, +0.170, +0.071, and +0.060, respectively. Ablation and sensitivity studies confirm that gains arise from trainability-aware compact circuit selection and expert fusion, not circuit scaling. Although classical baselines outperform on some tasks, fixed-split results show consistent improvements over the fixed hybrid reference. These analyses support the practical role of compact selection and fusion, with repeated-split and hardware-aware studies left for future work.

candidates.title: OrangeTree: A Linear and Tree-based Time Series Forecasting Model Supporting Multiple Input and Output Lengths
candidates.abstract: Time series forecasting (TSF) models suffer from a critical rigidity: the inability to handle Multiple Input and Output Lengths (MIOL) within a single architecture. Current workarounds, such as padding or autoregression, often incur computational redundancy or suffer from error accumulation. We propose OrangeTree, a linear and tree-based architecture that decouples model parameters from sequence lengths. It employs a Segment Tree Encoder and an Inverse Tree Decoder to translate multi-length input history into multi-length output predictions within a unified framework. Crucially, a Range Weighter and a Feature Fuser bridge these components, dynamically selecting and fusing relevant ranges into optimal contexts for forecasting. Experiments on six benchmarks confirm OrangeTree achieves the SOTA performance. In MIOL settings, it matches the accuracy of length-fixed models without substantial accuracy degradation or a substantial increase in inference latency typical of heuristic methods. Code is available at https://github.com/Tang-Yiqi/OrangeTree.

candidates.title: MIFLOW: Dynamic Recent-Behavior Priors for Reference-Calibrated Online Flow-Policy Reinforcement Learning
candidates.abstract: Flow-based policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous-control reinforcement learning. In online actor-critic learning, off-policy value estimates can be unreliable in poorly covered action regions, where expressive policies may shift probability mass toward critic-favored actions. We propose MIFLOW, which calibrates online flow-policy learning with a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior fitted to recently executed actions. Inspired by canalization as a qualitative analogy for path-dependent stabilization, we use the prior as a moving density reference for value-guided policy improvement. MIFLOW uses the approximate recent-action log-density in a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets. This correction increases the cost of low-density actions while keeping them available. Across six MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and five random seeds, MIFLOW achieves competitive mean return curves and higher late-training mean returns than the evaluated baselines on several tasks. In a Walker2d-v4 case study, MIFLOW shows a lower proportion of actions assigned low density by the learned reference, both overall and among high-Q actions. Prior-family and prior-buffer comparisons show task-dependent differences in returns and prior-defined diagnostics. These results support dynamic recent-behavior priors for reference calibration in the evaluated settings. The diagnostics measure how sampled actions align with the learned reference. True action support and critic extrapolation error remain unmeasured in these experiments.
candidates.comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE 38th International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI)

candidates.title: PreWAM: Exploring the Design of Latent Future Prediction for World-Action Modeling
candidates.abstract: World-action models combine action generation with future prediction, allowing visual transitions to serve as supervision for policy learning. Our controlled study of prediction spaces shows that spatially structured semantic features support better overall generalization under visual perturbations and make motion information more readily recoverable from learned predictive representations. Building on these observations, we introduce PreWAM, a world-action model that organizes future supervision around state changes in a prediction space defined by pretrained DINO features. Specifically, Residual World Prediction jointly learns source-relative changes and their resulting future states to emphasize dynamic information while preserving future-state semantics. Temporal-Scale Prediction conditions world queries on temporal distance to capture both short-term local motion and longer-horizon state evolution. These predictive objectives jointly shape a shared vision-language backbone with action supervision during pretraining and downstream policy learning. Experiments across the LIBERO benchmark family, SimplerEnv, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world robotic manipulation demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved generalization and robustness under diverse distribution shifts.

candidates.title: RESET: One Demonstration, One Verified World, Self-Improved Skills Across Embodiments
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents can iteratively self-improve robot manipulation skills in simulation benchmarks, yet real-world tasks provide neither ground-truth success scorers nor resettable practice environments. Our key observation is that a single real demonstration simultaneously specifies scene geometry, defines the terminal success criterion, and serves as a physical reference trajectory for verifying world fidelity---all decoupled from the source robot's kinematics. We present {RESET}: we reconstruct a contact-rich world and derive a frozen read-only criterion from one demonstration ({R}ebuild); check that world against the demonstration by open-loop replay and silhouette consistency ({E}xamine); evolve modular white-box task graphs and skill code from per-node failure evidence ({S}elf-improve); deploy frozen code on real robots with zero runtime LLM calls ({E}xecute); and share the verified world and criterion with unseen robots without new demonstrations ({T}ransfer). On 8 manipulation tasks, each rebuilt from one real demonstration, RESET achieves 97% average success on unseen layouts in simulation, whereas zero-shot code reaches 27%, per-task fine-tuned pi0.5 policies 31%, and Diffusion Policy 50%; injecting reconstruction defects shows that practice tolerates many reconstruction errors, that geometric errors can still stall or mislead it, and that the check flags most of them while physical randomization covers the rest. Without any target demonstrations, 3 heterogeneous robots acquire the same task skills in the shared world: a robot with similar arms copies 95% of its skill functions unchanged from the source robot, while robots with different arms and hands write their own. In real-robot experiments, the resulting programs run on 4 robots and succeed in 80% of 280 trials.

candidates.title: Cheap Memory Costs Future Compute: Co-Designing Persistent KV and GPU Execution for Efficient Streaming Video Diffusion
candidates.abstract: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).

candidates.title: HEAR, SEE, SPIKE ONCE: Highly Efficient NeuroAI Temporal Neural Networks for Low-Precision Multimodal Audio-Visual Classification and Online Learning
candidates.abstract: Spiking neural networks for multimodal audio-visual classification reach high accuracy by adopting deep-learning machinery: multi-stage convolutional or transformer encoders trained end-to-end with surrogate-gradient backpropagation through time. These prior works typically rely on full-precision (32-bit) parameters and do not treat hardware efficiency as a primary design objective. In this paper, we propose NeuTNN-AV, a much simpler hardware-amenable multimodal substrate built on the recently proposed NeuroAI Temporal Neural Network (NeuTNN) and demonstrate that it can match or outperform state-of-the-art SNN baselines with a fraction of their synapse counts. NeuTNN neurons carry multiple active dendritic segments. Each input line spikes at most once (temporal coding) and every weight is learned via a local reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule. All weights are 4-bit integers and inference uses only comparisons and additions. On CREMA-D, it reaches 78.6% with 2.34M synapses establishing a new state-of-the-art SNN accuracy, against 77.14% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). On UrbanSound8K-AV, NeuTNN reaches 98.82% with 1.38M synapses, against 96.85% for SMMT (9.99M parameters) and 98.96% for MISNet-XL (31M parameters). Weight memory is 23-106x smaller than the spiking baselines, and the measured synaptic energy per inference is two to three orders of magnitude lower. Furthermore, the proposed NeuTNN learns CREMA-D in a single pass with 73.8% accuracy and demonstrates rapid online continual learning by adapting to unseen actors from a few dozen clips.

candidates.title: Multi Agent Reinforcement Learning enhanced Federated Learning for Predicting Remaining Useful Lifetime
candidates.abstract: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction is central to Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). The growth of industrial IoT has unlocked large multivariate sensor streams and enabled deep models - especially Transformers - for long-horizon sequence learning. However, transformers are parameter-heavy and data-hungry, while operational datasets are often siloed and privacy-sensitive. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this by training across clients without raw data sharing, but in practice many clients connect over lossy wireless links where UDP is preferred for low latency, making model exchange vulnerable to packet drops. We present a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework that adapts FL to lossy channels by selecting per-client layer subsets to transmit and capping retransmissions. This framework is trained with QMIX value-function factorization for scalability. We instantiate the approach with a Graph Convolution Position-Aware Transformer (GCPATr) for RUL forecasting. On the CMAPSS dataset, our MARL-enhanced FL (RL-FL) consistently improves mean square error over standard FL, with the largest gains at high packet loss (e.g., up to 18% improvement on FD003 at 50% loss). These results show that MARL is an effective countermeasure to wireless degradation in FL-based RUL prediction.

candidates.title: EEG-Jev: A Unified Single-Pass Decision Model for EEG
candidates.abstract: EEG analysis spans choosing alternatives, judging statements, and rating ordered attributes, requiring calibratable probabilities with explicit meaning. We present EEG-Jev, a unified single-pass decision model for EEG. Given an EEG window, a question and an answer specification, one forward pass returns a typed readout: CHOICE gives a candidate distribution, NOUL a proposition probability, and SCORE an ordered-level distribution and expectation. One checkpoint is trained jointly and evaluated once on held-out splits of 35 public sources. Core raw outputs reach 54.08% balanced accuracy on Stieger2021 motor imagery, 70.45% on Sleep-EDF-SC sleep staging, 72.11% per window at threshold 0.5 on CHB-MIT seizure detection with 0.825 AUROC, and 1.700 MAE on 0-10 ds005292 pain ratings. Prior correction and temperature scaling lower negative log-likelihood from 0.766 to 0.606 on Sleep-EDF-SC and 0.166 to 0.019 on CHB-MIT, while direct readout cuts batch-1 latency from 122.43 to 63.11 ms (1.94-fold) against a matched-backbone generative comparator. Interactive demonstration and aggregate results: https://neuroimglab.github.io/EEG-Jev/.

candidates.title: RepoEviAgent: Scalable Synthesis of Evidence-Grounded Repository-Level Question Answering Tasks
candidates.abstract: Real-world software engineering (SWE) tasks require agents to understand repository structures, cross-module dependencies, and runtime behaviors, posing significant challenges for constructing high-quality training and evaluation data. To address this, we propose RepoEviAgent, a scalable SWE data construction framework that integrates quality-aware data curation and role-specialized multi-agent task synthesis. Starting from 8,477 open-source repositories and approximately 2.48 million pull request records, we employ semantic alignment, complexity constraints, and multidimensional quality assessment to identify valuable SWE data. We further develop a sandbox-based multi-agent framework that integrates automated environment construction, execution validation, repository exploration, and evidence-grounded Q&A synthesis. Based on this framework, we construct RepoEviQA, a benchmark for Repository-Level Evidence-Grounded Question Answering, comprising 334 tasks across five programming languages and diverse SWE categories, with rigorous rubric-based evaluation. We evaluate five frontier coding models on RepoEviQA, revealing substantial performance differences across task categories and programming languages.

candidates.title: Subliminal Learning Crosses Modalities
candidates.abstract: Subliminal learning refers to a surprising phenomenon in language models wherein a prompt given to one model (e.g., preference for cats) can be subliminally distilled to another model via training on data that is ostensibly meaningless (e.g., number sequences). This paper shows that text-based subliminal learning transfers cross-modally, in particular, a topic/preference (e.g., animals) transferred through number sequences across vision-language models also changes how images are generated and represented. First, we show that a diffusion model using the student as its text encoder generates the student's animal more often than with the original model as its text encoder, but not its color or style. We then investigate the mechanism behind this phenomenon and which concepts transfer across modalities. A constant component of the student's change accounts for much of the shift of image representations toward the trait. Adding this component uniformly can change the generated animal, which depends on the whole prompt, but not concepts such as color or style, which are encoded in a single token. Finally, we introduce weight lens as an approach to identify a subliminal trait from the weights of a single trained model, and show that it identifies the trait of nearly every student, including traits that do not surface in generated images.

candidates.title: CALVIN-MAX: When Does a Mid-Execution Change Hurt a Robot Policy?
candidates.abstract: Robots must often keep working after the world changes, as when a block moves or the camera shifts while the robot still acts on what it saw before. Recent work showed that one change during a task lowers success for every policy tested, but did not separate the effect of its timing from the cost of the changed world, or measure what it costs afterwards. We introduce CALVIN-MAX, a benchmark of 7,828 cases on CALVIN's five-instruction chains, each with one change to the objects, the camera, the robot, or the instruction. Each case compares three runs that are identical until the affected instruction begins: one without the change, one with it in place from that moment, and one in which it arrives while the robot is moving. The second run against the first gives the cost of the changed world, and the third against the second the effect of meeting it mid-motion. On 1,526 held-out cases per policy, with hypotheses fixed in advance, each of ten released policies loses 4.4 to 9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction over the eight core changes. Whether timing matters depends on the change: one that alters what the robot sees costs 5.4 points less mid-motion than from the start, whereas a change to the scene itself or to the robot shows no detectable effect. Rewinding the robot to the start of the instruction removes the benefit for every policy; the stricter test we fixed in advance, that the rewound run then matches the second run, passes for three. The cost also outlasts the affected instruction: the change stays in place, and a policy that still completes that instruction is 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.
candidates.comment: 34 pages (8-page main paper and 23-page supplementary material), 19 figures, 28 tables. Project page: https://forall-labs.github.io/CALVIN-MAX/

candidates.title: No Fixed Configuration Is Best: Context- and Cost-Aware Tuning of LLM Pipelines, with an Application to Schema Matching and Mapping
candidates.abstract: The numeric settings of a multi-stage LLM pipeline (a compound AI system) are the usual target of tuning. We tuned all of them for an LLM pipeline for schema matching and mapping, with accuracy and cost as joint objectives, and we show what this buys, what it cannot buy, and where the remaining accuracy is. First, tuning buys cost and a little accuracy. On 35 tasks, with whole groups of tasks held out from tuning, one tuned configuration gains 2.9 points of top-1 accuracy (HR@1) over the default at 18% more cost, and another keeps the accuracy of the default at 32% lower cost. Second, the accuracy depends on a choice that numeric tuning cannot reach. Restricting the search for each source column to one assigned target table changes HR@1 by +30 points on a MIMIC-III to OMOP task and by -52 points on a task built from database views, more than numeric tuning gains on nine of ten test tasks. Neither setting is right for all tasks: on the larger set of 41 tasks used for the remaining results, mean HR@1 is 75.7% with the restriction (the default) and 83.1% without it. Third, choosing the setting per task is not enough either: even an oracle that picks the better setting for each task reaches only 87.8% on the 41 tasks, because the better setting differs between the columns of one task. The pipeline therefore runs both settings, and an LLM judge chooses among their candidate answers on the 26% of columns on which they disagree. This reaches 91.5% HR@1 on the 41 tasks, at 5.9 times the cost of the default, about one cent per column.

candidates.title: Ada-BFM: Adapting Behavior Foundation Models for Humanoid Scene Interaction
candidates.abstract: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose humanoid control through pretraining on large-scale behavioral data. However, their proficiency in whole-body coordination does not readily extend to scene interaction, which requires adapting motion to scene-dependent geometric constraints and contact dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce Ada-BFM, a post-training framework that adapts pretrained BFMs for humanoid scene interaction. Ada-BFM augments the original architecture with a lightweight adapter, enabling interaction-specific adjustments while leveraging pretrained control capabilities. Rather than producing a separate controller for each task, the framework yields a shared model for each interaction domain, supporting diverse tasks involving terrain or object interaction. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate that Ada-BFM enables diverse scene interaction behaviors, accelerates learning compared with training from scratch, and largely preserves pretrained behavioral competence. These findings establish Ada-BFM as an effective and efficient approach to extending the capabilities of BFMs beyond their pretraining settings while retaining their strengths in general whole-body control.

candidates.title: Start Where the Data Are: Statistical Priors for One-Step Generation on Manifolds
candidates.abstract: Fast generation on manifolds is important for scientific applications such as protein design, yet existing one-step generators often produce spurious samples in low-density gaps between data modes. Our analysis highlights the mismatch between uniform noise and concentrated data, motivating a statistical prior that captures the data's coarse structure. We first estimate this prior by fitting mixtures of tangent-space Gaussians through geometry-aware moment matching. However, independent noise-data pairing can still connect different modes and weaken the benefit of the fitted prior. We therefore introduce posterior coupling, which samples a latent component conditioned on each data point and draws its paired noise from that component. To extend this approach to long torsion-angle chains, where full-covariance mixtures become costly, we use a hidden Markov prior to model sequential dependence with shared parameters. The resulting framework plugs into existing one-step training pipelines while retaining the generator architecture, training objective, and single network evaluation at inference. Experiments on spheres, tori, and SO(3) demonstrate substantial improvements across multiple generators, reducing distributional error by up to $125\times$ and the protein Ramachandran outlier rate from 12.1% to 0.55%.
candidates.comment: 33 pages (8 main + references + 22 supplementary), 22 figures, 24 tables. Code: https://github.com/olivia3395/statprior-onestep

candidates.title: Explainable Deep Learning for Malaria Parasite Detection and Species Differentiation in Thick Blood Smear Images: A Pilot Feasibility Study
candidates.abstract: Species-level differentiation of Plasmodium falciparum (PF) and P. vivax (PV) determines treatment, yet deep learning detectors rarely test whether their explanations are reliable. In this pilot feasibility study of TRACE-Mal, a research prototype combining YOLOv8n-seg detection and a six-model soft-voting ensemble, we examined whether agreement among three post-hoc explanation methods (Grad-CAM, LIME and SHAP) is associated with the correctness of species calls. the study analysed 2,847 parasite crops from 250 thick smears within publicly available Lacuna Malaria Datasets. The model achieved an mAP50 score of 0.79 and the ensemble had a macro F1 of 0.84 (PF recall 0.86; PV recall 0.74). Unadjusted analyses of crops revealed that predictions explained by greather than or equal to 2 methods were more accurate (86.2% vs 78.9%; difference 7.3 percentage points; 95% CI 3.5-11.1) compared to those explained by less than 2 methods. As the number of explanatory methods increased so did prediction accuracy (from 73.8% for no methods to 89.5% for all three methods). When performing a cluster-bootstrap analysis of 60 test images, again there was a positive consensus difference (7.3 percentage points; 95% CI 2.9-11.8). Further, incorporating explanation information into a model's prediction confidence enhanced its error differentiation ability (AUROC 0.024; 95% CI 0.008-0.041). PF and PV parasite crops have distinct morphologies. Although based on one unvalidated public data source, these findings demonstrate proof-of-concept and should not be taken as a measure of diagnostic capability.

candidates.title: Modeling Event-Conditioned Emotional Expression Response with LLM Agents in a Synthetic Social Simulation
candidates.abstract: Emotions are central drivers of human behavior, yet most behavioral models fail to capture their role in shaping perception, decision-making, and collective action. Application areas such as emergency response and public health are especially constrained by the lack of emotion-aware modeling. While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into agent-based models (ABMs), little work has examined how to endow LLM agents with emotional reasoning or validated their ability to reproduce empirically observed emotional patterns. This study addresses this gap by introducing a hierarchical prompting framework that conditions LLM agents with demographic, psychological, and contextual cues to generate event-conditioned emotional responses to real-world events. We validate the resulting event-conditioned emotional responses against large-scale social media reaction data derived from the Social Science One Facebook URL Shares Dataset, complemented by demographic and personality benchmarks. Our simulation results reproduce both polarized and consensus-driven emotional patterns with significant fidelity, supporting the application of LLM agents for emotion-aware modeling in behavioral simulations. We also find, however, that systematic gaps in emotional expression of LLM agents and human populations exist, such as the underexpression of anger relative to human baselines. As such, these findings highlight the need for continued calibration if LLM agents are to serve as proxies for human populations in behavioral modeling. By quantifying their divergence from human populations in terms of emotional expression, we hope that our methods can aid in this effort.

candidates.title: Two-Stage Post-Training for Flow-Based Embodied Foundation Models
candidates.abstract: Large-scale pretraining provides embodied models with general capabilities, but reliable task execution still requires post training. In multitask settings, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) faces distribution mismatch between training and deployment, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) is limited by sparse rewards and uneven learning progress across tasks. Multi-teacher on policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates expert capabilities through dense supervision on the model's own trajectories, but achieving performance beyond the teachers remains challenging. We propose a two-stage post training framework for flow-based embodied models, constructing distillation objectives from the velocity regression formulation of conditional flow matching. Stage 1 efficiently consolidates expert capabilities through MOPD. Stage 2 combines RL with teacher distillation that weights velocity errors according to the sampling noise, where distillation is restricted to failed trajectories to supplement sparse rewards with dense guidance without directly constraining successful behaviors. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show that the framework outperforms joint SFT and exceeds the corresponding teachers' aggregate success rates. Sample efficiency comparisons show higher success rates than direct RL with fewer environment interactions.

candidates.title: Faithful Persona Steering under Incongruity via Dual-Stream Refinement
candidates.abstract: Standard LLM personalization typically frames identity as a static retrieval task, overlooking the inherent incongruity of human personas, where stable traits coexist with atypical, context-specific stances. Existing methods struggle to reconcile these dimensions: prompting succumbs to context drift over long sequences, while fine-tuning often suppresses idiosyncratic "quirks" in favor of generic distributional patterns. To bridge this gap, we present QuirkyMind, a framework that disentangles identity definition from its expression. First, Traits Anchoring constructs a dual-stream latent state, fusing a sentence-level summary for semantic stability with a token-level sequence for generative control. This state is stabilized via In-Context Narrative Refinement using an alternating objective: a discriminative InfoNCE loss anchors the persona in representation space to prevent drift, while a generative cross-entropy loss ensures faithful verbalization. Finally, Persona Steered Generalization transfers the refined state to downstream tasks via parameter-efficient adapters. Empirical evaluations on Persona-Steered QA and Narrative Inference demonstrate that QuirkyMind mitigates drift, consolidating persona knowledge without erasing authentic incongruities.
candidates.comment: Accepted to Findings of ACL 2026. 18 pages, 14 figures, 8 tables

candidates.title: BendGS: Observation-Conditioned Gaussian Self-Modeling for Continuum Robots
candidates.abstract: Visual self-models learn from images how a robot moves under motor commands. Continuum robots need them even more, as they bend continuously without measured joint angles or fixed link geometry. Existing continuum self-models predict point clouds, image-space curves, or future images, but not the next 3D shape, appearance, and tip pose together from an observed body. 3D Gaussians offer a renderable representation of shape and appearance, yet articulated Gaussian self-models rely on joint angles to drive deformation. In this work, we propose BendGS, which uses a virtual backbone estimated from observation to drive command-conditioned Gaussian deformation, enabling next-state prediction for continuum robots without measured joint angles. In Gaussian modeling, a feed-forward network reconstructs the robot as 3D Gaussians from multi-view images, and the backbone, a chain of coordinate frames, is fitted to back-projected depth points to estimate the bending state. In transition, a network predicts its change under a relative motor command to deform the bound Gaussians. The deformed Gaussians render the next images and the 3D shape, and the distal frame gives the tip pose. Training losses use RGB-D images and masks, without bending or tip labels. On simulated and real robots, BendGS achieves the lowest Chamfer distance, best image quality, and lowest tip errors among the compared methods.

candidates.title: Co-DRIS: Physics-Informed Predictive Belief and Variable-Impedance Learning for Reactive Catching under Coupled Uncertainty
candidates.abstract: Reactive robotic manipulation is acutely sensitive to simultaneous sensing noise, measurement dropouts, joint execution errors, and contact parameter variations. While single-frame frameworks like Domain-Randomized Instance Set (DRIS) achieve strong robustness under isolated uncertainties (86.4%), they degrade severely when perception and actuation uncertainties co-occur (27.6% across 10 coupled stress scenarios) due to memoryless encoding and fixed high-stiffness PD control.
